summary: An April 1st joke RFC written in mock archaic English. It supplies a collection of ASCII art creatures for authors to reuse in documents, with a tongue-in-cheek history of ASCII. It is humor, not a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8140 is an April 1st joke collection of pictures made from ASCII characters. It presents creatures and structures in mock-archaic prose and is not a protocol specification.

questions: what is the arte of ascii
subtitle: An April 1st collection of ASCII pictures, described in mock-archaic prose.

tldr.problem: This April 1st joke imagines document authors wanting reusable pictures made from ASCII characters.
tldr.mechanism: It presents a mock-scholarly collection of ASCII art showing creatures and structures, with deliberately fanciful descriptions.
tldr.outcome: The document supplies humorous examples for amusement. Its mock history and security discussion are part of the joke, not technical guidance.

today: RFC 8140 is an Informational document published on April 1, 2017. It is a humorous collection of ASCII art and does not specify a protocol.

sections.title: A Humorous Collection
sections.content: This April 1st document supplies textual representations of “all manner of things” that authors might reuse. Its introduction jokes that Gutenberg discovered ASCII and describes the character set as a source of visual art. The historical claims are part of the document's humor.
sections.plainLanguage: This April 1st joke collects pictures made from text characters. Its claims about the history of ASCII are deliberately playful.

sections.title: Creatures and Structures in Characters
sections.content: The collection groups its pictures as Beasts of the Land, Creatures of the Deep, Spirits of the Air, and Man-Made Structures. Examples include a troll, unicorn, Loch Ness Monster, swordfish, vampire, avian carriers, Bauhaus shapes, and a gingerbread house.
sections.plainLanguage: The text pictures include creatures, birds, shapes, and a house. They are drawn with ordinary characters rather than image files.

sections.title: Mock Security and IANA Sections
sections.content: The RFC continues the joke with sections on IANA, security, manageability, and morality. The security section includes ASCII pictures of a key, a lock, and a backdoor; the IANA section jokes that a registry might track colors assigned to shapes. These sections provide humor rather than operational instructions.
sections.plainLanguage: The formal-sounding security and IANA sections are also jokes. They include more text drawings and do not define network behavior.
